_why: Frames a generator cannot draw from their pose, held on a neighbour at pack time. Each entry names the layer, the clip, the facing and the frame, and the frame that stands in for it. Owner, 2026-09-26: the south draw's frame five melted the head on two male seeds and on the female base - the bow arm points at the camera across the face.
_why_male_cape_long: 2026-09-26: the generator drew the cape inconsistently in three places, each found by counting the cape's pixels per frame and looking at every row that shrank by half. The north-west attack collapsed it to a shoulder mantle for three frames of the swing; the north-east attack dissolved it into specks for one; the north walk dropped it for the last two frames of the stride, a pop on every step. A keyed cape carries no body, so holding a neighbour cannot ghost a limb. Rows that shrank because the cape is swinging were looked at and left alone. Later the same day: the back-view idle drew the cape closed for three frames and open, as if seen from the front, for five - a flicker on every breath, missed because the scan compared each frame with its row's median and the row was mostly wrong. Each open frame holds the closed frame whose body pose is nearest, measured off the base layer.
_why_female_cape_long: 2026-09-26: the same fault as the male's, in the loops a player watches from behind. In the back view the generator drew the cape open - arranged as if seen from the front - for five frames of the idle, six of the walk and four of the sprint, so it flickered closed and open every cycle. The idle and the walk hold the closed frame whose body pose is nearest, measured off the base layer; the sprint repeats its first half-stride, because a back-view stride is the same sway on either leg and holding one frame froze the cape for half the cycle. One-shots keep their open frames: in a swing the cape flung aside reads as the motion.
